items.prompt: Two updates contain the exact same facts about a delay, but one leads with the reason and the other leads with the impact. Per L2, why does the ordering matter if the facts are identical?
choices: It doesn't matter — readers process both orderings identically

Leading with the reason forces the reader to evaluate whether the excuse is good enough before knowing what it costs them; leading with impact lets them assess what matters to them immediately, with the reason as context afterward
Leading with the reason is always more honest, since it shows the full reasoning first
Ordering only matters in written updates, not spoken ones
items.explanation: The content can be identical while the reading experience differs sharply — reason-first structurally reads as justification before information, which is exactly why even a fully legitimate reason can come across as an excuse purely because of order.

items.prompt: Why is "should be done soon" identified as the most common trust-eroding pattern, even when the person saying it genuinely believes it?
choices: Because it's always a lie
Because it's vague and unfalsifiable — a string of "soon"s that don't hold up is indistinguishable, from the reader's side, from someone with no real handle on the situation, regardless of good faith
Because it uses casual language instead of formal language
Because it doesn't include an apology
items.explanation: The problem isn't dishonesty in the moment — it's that vague, unfalsifiable estimates give the reader no way to calibrate trust, and repeated misses without a specific, checkable claim erode confidence regardless of whether each individual update felt honest when written.

items.prompt: What's the practical benefit of explicitly labeling a claim as "known" (confirmed) versus "estimated" (a projection) in a status update?
choices: It has no practical benefit, it's just more formal-sounding

It tells the reader how much weight to put on each claim, and gives both the reader and the future writer a specific, checkable reason if an estimate turns out wrong, rather than a vague sense the update was "wrong somehow"
It's required by most corporate style guides
It only matters for legal liability reasons
items.explanation: Per L2, separating known from estimated is what lets an update be genuinely honest while still conveying confidence where warranted — an unmarked mix of confirmed facts and projections is exactly where optimism bias quietly turns into something that reads as dishonest in hindsight.

items.prompt: Per L2's last section, why is staying silent during a period of real uncertainty described as a trust cost, not a neutral choice?
choices: Because silence is technically a form of lying

Because silence gets filled in by the reader's own assumptions, which are rarely more generous than the truth — the same eventual delay surfaced incrementally reads very differently from the identical delay surfacing as one late surprise
Because company policy requires updates every single day without exception
Because silence is only a problem if the news turns out to be bad
items.explanation: Frequency is treated as a trust variable independent of content — the underlying facts can be identical, but a team that surfaces uncertainty as it develops reads as on top of the situation, while the same team going quiet until a surprise reads as either blindsided or withholding, even if that's not actually true.

items.prompt: In L3, Path A and Path B both eventually took about the same total time to ship the feature. What was actually different between the two paths?
choices: Path B's engineer was faster and more skilled at the technical work

The update discipline: Path A repeated a vague, unfalsifiable projection three times without naming what was actually uncertain; Path B named the real uncertainty once with a specific number, and only sent further updates when something genuinely new was confirmed
Path A's delay was caused by a harder technical problem than Path B's
Path B simply didn't communicate about the delay at all, avoiding the issue
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that the underlying technical difficulty and total elapsed time were the same in both paths — this is a story about communication discipline, not technical speed, which is exactly why the same set of facts produced such different trust outcomes.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes, why did Path B's mid-week-3 update avoid becoming another empty "just checking in" message?
choices: Because it was scheduled automatically regardless of content

Because it only went out once something genuinely changed and was confirmed (the redesigned retry logic was done and tested) — an update with no new confirmed fact trains readers to skim, which defeats the purpose the next time something actually needs attention
Because it repeated the same root-cause explanation from the previous update for reinforcement
Because it included a long apology, which readers expect on a schedule
items.explanation: L3's second failure mode warns specifically against re-explaining the same root cause with no new information — Path B's updates were triggered by genuinely new confirmed facts, not a fixed schedule, which is what kept each one worth reading closely.
